title: What you're unsure of
hook: uncertainty is part of the path
tomorrow: how short can a prayer in the Torah be?

segments.voice: A week of endings and beginnings: grief has a shape, answer amen, remember well, your beliefs, your practices, where you belong. Yesterday's picture: sometimes two people and a book are enough.
screen: `SIX LINES, ONE WEEK.` → `TWO PEOPLE AND A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Every group project has a moment when someone finally says "i actually don't know," and the whole room relaxes. Noa hit that moment with her roommate form. She wrote her three beliefs, then got to the big one, what happens after we die, and left it blank. Is a blank allowed, in a tradition that loves answers?
screen: `"I ACTUALLY DON'T KNOW."` → `ONE LINE LEFT BLANK.` → `IS A BLANK ALLOWED?`

segments.voice: It is, and the tradition says so itself. Deuteronomy draws the line: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God." Some things are given to people to know and do; some are not. The Talmud lives by this. Sometimes a long argument ends without a winner, in one word: teiku, let it stand. The question stays open, on the page, for the next reader. And the Talmud gives advice for the tongue: teach it to say "I do not know." This week held a lot of that. Grief that has a shape but no answers. A prayer that praises when nothing makes sense. Beliefs written as sure, growing, testing. Unsure isn't the opposite of a path. Said honestly, it's one of the steps on it. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud sometimes ends an argument with a single word that means let it stand.
screen: `THE SECRET THINGS BELONG TO GOD.` · `TEIKU: LET IT STAND.` · `TEACH YOUR TONGUE: I DON'T KNOW.` · then, large: `UNSURE IS HONEST.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let one uncertainty come up, something you honestly don't know. Don't argue with it or solve it. Let it stand, the way the Talmud does, and stay with it quietly for the rest of the time.
screen: `ONE HONEST UNCERTAINTY.` · `DON'T SOLVE IT.` · `LET IT STAND.`

segments.voice: What you're unsure of: the questions you honestly can't close yet. The Talmud has a word for leaving one open: teiku.
For the road: unsure is honest, and the tradition left room for it. That's a week of your own path.

screen: `DAY 1771 COUNTS.` → `YOUR OWN PATH · 4 OF 10.` → `TOMORROW: HOW SHORT CAN A PRAYER IN THE TORAH BE?`
